findings.claim: The OIDC attestation architectural commitment (MAJ-SAFE-001 fix) specifies 'verifies against GitHub's OIDC JWKS' for adopter emit verification. OIDC JWKS verification is signature-only: it proves GitHub signed the OIDC JWT, but does not prove the attested artifact was produced by the SCP reusable workflow at the expected SHA pin. The GitHub Actions OIDC token and artifact attestation mechanism (Sigstore/Fulcio) binds the artifact digest to an OIDC identity including job_workflow_ref — but ONLY if the verifier explicitly checks that claim. Without an explicit aggregator-side check of job_workflow_ref against the pinned SCP reusable workflow SHA, any workflow in an opted-in adopter's repo can produce a valid OIDC attestation that passes the aggregator's verification. A malicious adopter can create a custom workflow, generate a fabricated scorecard-emit.json (verdict:allow, empty rule_counts), attest it via gh attestation/actions/attest, and have the aggregator accept it as a legitimate SCP reusable workflow emit.
findings.evidence: Plan-doc §5 step 3 (fix-round-1 wording): 'the SCP reusable workflow uses GitHub Actions Artifact Attestation (OIDC-based) — the per-PR run signs the emit with the GitHub Actions OIDC token at upload time; the aggregator verifies against GitHub's OIDC JWKS.' The phrase 'verifies against GitHub's OIDC JWKS' specifies only signature verification (was this JWT issued by GitHub's OIDC provider?), not claim verification (was this artifact produced by the expected workflow at the expected SHA?). GitHub Actions Artifact Attestation uses Sigstore/Fulcio: the Fulcio certificate embeds OIDC claims including job_workflow_ref (e.g. 'jrnb2024/standards-control-plane-/.github/workflows/policy-check.yml@refs/heads/main'); the gh attestation verify command accepts --owner and --repo filters but does NOT by default verify job_workflow_ref against a specific workflow path or SHA. D-042 reservation in §9 of plan-doc: 'D-042 — 023C: Aggregator pipeline trust model — GitHub Actions Artifact Attestation (OIDC-based) for adopter emits + SCP-side Ed25519 key registry.' No constraint on which OIDC claims the aggregator must verify is named in the D-042 reservation. §4 threat boundary 1 states 'the adopter cannot tamper with the emit content' because 'the SCP reusable workflow (D-022 SHA-pinned)' generates it — this claim is false without job_workflow_ref claim verification.
findings.impact: A malicious opted-in adopter (i.e. a repo listed in docs/scorecards/opt-in-registry.yaml via a CODEOWNERS-gated PR, which is an existing trust barrier) can inject false compliance data into the estate scorecard index. Concretely: create a GitHub Actions workflow that writes scorecard-emit.json with verdict:allow and zero findings, attest it, and the aggregator's OIDC-JWKS-only check passes. The estate scorecard would then report that repo as fully compliant regardless of its actual policy-check results. This undermines the entire purpose of estate-wide observability and directly bypasses the bypass-surface defense that MAJ-SAFE-001's fix was intended to establish. The bypass requires a deliberately malicious adopted party, not an external attacker; but the threat boundary 1 mitigation ('the adopter cannot tamper') is precisely the property that is invalidated.
findings.mitigation: Add a non-negotiable content constraint to the D-042 reservation block in both §9 of the plan-doc and docs/DECISIONS.md header note: 'The aggregator MUST verify the job_workflow_ref OIDC claim in each artifact attestation against the expected SCP reusable workflow path and SHA pin (the same SHA pin used in the adopter's caller wrapper). OIDC JWKS signature verification alone is insufficient — a JWKS-only check proves GitHub issued the token but does not prove the SCP reusable workflow produced the artifact. The gh attestation verify implementation in 023C MUST include a --deny-self-signed flag (or equivalent) plus a claim-assertion step that rejects any attestation whose job_workflow_ref does not match the expected workflow path + SHA.' This is an inline-fix to the D-042 reservation wording in §9 (plan-doc) and the DECISIONS.md header note at lines 12–21. No descope.

findings.claim: Invariant 6 states 'Closes the bypass-surface concern that a compromised aggregator could mis-report estate state.' This claim is accurate for a compromised aggregator PIPELINE (in-flight emit substitution is caught by per-emit OIDC attestations; in-flight index fabrication without the SCP signing key would fail consumer verification). However the claim does not hold for a compromised aggregator SIGNING KEY. If the SCP-side Ed25519 private key (held as a GitHub Actions secret in the SCP repo, per WP-SCP-021 D-024) is extracted or leaked, an adversary can sign a fabricated central index that passes all consumer Ed25519 verification. The threat model in §4 excludes 'operator-side trojan attack on the SCP repo' under bus-factor-1, but key material leakage (e.g. via a compromised third-party action in .github/**, a secrets-scanning miss, or runner environment inspection) is a distinct attack vector that does not require operator-level repo access.
findings.evidence: Plan-doc §2 invariant 6: 'Aggregator output is Ed25519-signed. Each emit + the central index carry an Ed25519 signature using the same key infrastructure WP-SCP-021 established for MCP receipts. A tampered index can be detected by signature-verification at consumption time. Closes the bypass-surface concern that a compromised aggregator could mis-report estate state.' Plan-doc §4 threat model exclusion: 'Operator-side trojan attack on the SCP repo — bus-factor-1 cost acknowledged in invariant 7; mitigated by the 2026-07-21 quarterly review + CODEOWNERS coverage on output/scorecards/**.' docs/security/mcp-signing-keys.pub is a placeholder with no key entry yet (6 comment lines only, no (key_id, public_key, valid_from, valid_until) row). D-024 establishes 'SCP_MCP_PRIVATE_KEY in secrets' as the key storage mechanism; the private key lives as a GitHub Actions repository secret. A third-party action with access to the runner environment (cf. .github/** CODEOWNERS protection, which guards the workflow YAML but not runtime secrets extraction) represents a plausible key-compromise path distinct from operator trojan.
findings.impact: A compromised aggregator signing key allows an adversary to: (1) fabricate a central index.json with any desired estate-compliance picture, (2) sign it with the known private key, (3) push it to the repo via any write path (including opening a PR that passes CI since the signature is valid). Consumer Ed25519 verification passes. The markdown report and MCP method both serve the fabricated data. The CODEOWNERS PR-layer defense provides notice (PR routes to @jrnb2024) but in single-operator count=0 mode a PR can self-merge. This is worse than the pipeline-compromise scenario because signature verification — the last active control — is neutralised.
findings.mitigation: File TF-023A-003 for 023C. Add a clarifying sentence to invariant 6: 'This signature scheme closes the pipeline-compromise bypass (fabricated emits injected mid-flight) but not the signing-key-compromise bypass (key material extraction enabling offline forgery). Key material compromise is mitigated by GitHub Actions secrets isolation, CODEOWNERS coverage on .github/**, and the 2026-07-21 quarterly review; it is not mitigated by the signature scheme itself.' This scoping makes the residual risk explicit to 023C implementers and aligns invariant 6's coverage claim with its actual security property. Additionally, D-042 should specify that the aggregator signing key is a repository secret (not embedded in workflow YAML), and that key compromise triggers the same coordinated disclosure path as SECURITY.md. No descope.

findings.claim: Fix-round-1 added a positive faithfulness commitment to invariant 1: 'the aggregator MUST faithfully report verified emit content — it does not transform, smooth, or best-interpret verdicts; rule_counts and waiver counts are passed through as-emitted from each adopter's signed emit. A divergence between the aggregator's reported state and an adopter's actual output/findings/policy-check-summary.json is a verification failure, not a smoothing artefact.' This commitment is not reflected in §6's 023C acceptance criteria. The 023C ACs read: 'Aggregator runs on the SCP repo against an empty registry without error; aggregator opens a draft PR template; D-042 filed.' A Codex executor dispatched for 023C can satisfy these ACs while implementing silent suppression (dropping unverifiable emits without marking them verification_failure), silent verdict coercion (treating warn as allow), or pass-through only for allow-verdicts — none of which would fail the stated ACs.
findings.evidence: Plan-doc §2 invariant 1 (fix-round-1 addition): 'Positively: the aggregator MUST faithfully report verified emit content — it does not transform, smooth, or best-interpret verdicts; rule_counts and waiver counts are passed through as-emitted.' Plan-doc §6 slice 023C acceptance criteria: 'Aggregator runs on the SCP repo against an empty registry without error; aggregator opens a draft PR template; D-042 filed.' No AC requires a canary test with a known-verdict emit. FIX-ROUND-1.md fix 9: 'docs/plans/WP-SCP-023-cross-repo-scorecards.md invariant 1: aggregator-faithfulness positive commitment (COMP-MIN-004).' The fix was an inline-doc change that did not update 023C's acceptance criteria to operationalise the commitment. Plan-doc §5 failure modes for the aggregator: 'Emit signature invalid → adopter row marked verification_failure... Aggregator-side error → the cron run fails loudly; no partial-index commit lands.' These failure-mode behaviours are not in 023C's ACs either.
findings.impact: Without a faithfulness AC, a Codex executor implementing 023C could: (a) silently drop rows for adopters whose emits fail OIDC verification (instead of marking verification_failure as invariant 1 requires), resulting in an index that appears clean for an adopter with tampered emits; (b) implement verdict coercion (treat all non-deny emits as allow), making the estate scorecard falsely optimistic; (c) suppress the waivers_aggregate fields from row output, breaking the cross-estate waiver-count observability WP-SCP-023 exists to provide. All three would satisfy '023C runs without error; opens a draft PR; D-042 filed.' The positive faithfulness commitment is the load-bearing constraint for the slice's correctness; without an AC that verifies it, the commitment is aspirational rather than enforced.
findings.mitigation: Add to §6 slice 023C acceptance criteria: '(AC-023C-faithfulness) Given a fixture emit with a known verdict (deny) and known rule_counts, the aggregator output row reports the identical verdict and counts without transformation; (AC-023C-verification-failure) Given a fixture emit with an invalid OIDC attestation (or invalid Ed25519 signature for any SCP-side path), the aggregator marks the adopter row verification_failure rather than dropping the row or defaulting to allow; (AC-023C-failure-modes) An aggregator-side error causes the cron run to fail loudly with no partial-index commit.' This is an inline-fix to §6 of the plan-doc. No descope.

findings.claim: TF-023A-001 (filed for MIN-SAFE-006 k-anonymity framing mismatch) defers clarification to 'when WP-SCP-024 cascade slice begins.' But the markdown report that creates the per-repo disclosure surface (the actual scope of the mismatch — per-row expiring_within_30d counts are visible regardless of estate-level k-anonymity) is created in slice 023D, not WP-SCP-024. The TF trigger timing is misaligned: a 023D Codex executor dispatched without TF-023A-001 resolved will implement the per-adopter-row disclosure surface without the k-anonymity-vs-per-row clarification the TF is intended to drive.
findings.evidence: FIX-ROUND-1.md TF-forwards section: 'TF-023A-001 (low priority): clarify R-023-01 k-anonymity mitigation framing when WP-SCP-024 cascade slice begins.' Plan-doc §5 exposure surface: 'Adopter table: repo | scp_version | verdict | rule denies | active waivers | expiring waivers | rule-config disabled.' The expiring waivers column exposes expiring_within_30d per adopter row in the markdown report generated in 023D. R-023-01 forward-compat mitigation references slice 024 for k-anonymity — but the markdown report is the primary per-repo disclosure surface and is created in 023D. WP-SCP-024 is described as estate cascade, not privacy controls.
findings.impact: Nit-level: the TF timing means the per-row vs aggregate-k-anonymity framing is unresolved when 023D ships. The per-adopter-row disclosure in the markdown report will be implemented without explicit documentation that it is intentionally visible to the SCP operator (CODEOWNERS-bounded) and that k-anonymity applies only to aggregate MCP metrics. The R-023-01 risk mitigation in the plan-doc remains imprecise through 023D. No active bypass surface — the disclosure is intentional and CODEOWNERS-bounded.
findings.mitigation: Update TF-023A-001 trigger from 'when WP-SCP-024 begins' to 'at 023D kickoff.' At 023D, R-023-01 should be amended to explicitly distinguish: (a) per-adopter-row markdown report — intentionally visible to SCP operator; access-controlled by SCP repo CODEOWNERS; k-anonymity does not apply; (b) aggregate MCP metrics — k-anonymity forward-compat applies if leakage proves material. Add explicit note: 'if the SCP repo is public-readable, per-repo expiring_within_30d counts are public; this should be documented in the 023D onboarding section of ADOPT-001 §13.' One-line update to FIX-ROUND-1.md TF entry or inline note on R-023-01 in plan-doc.

summary: All five R1 safety findings (MAJ-SAFE-001, MAJ-SAFE-002, MAJ-SAFE-003, MIN-SAFE-005, COMP-MAJ-002) are verified closed at the plan-doc level against actual repo state at HEAD 94d096e. CODEOWNERS ordering invariant holds: src/** (line 50), docs/scorecards/** (line 58), and output/scorecards/** (line 59) are all inserted before /CODEOWNERS self-protection (line 122). Key registry model correctly scopes rotation handling to the SCP-side aggregator-emitted index (Ed25519), while adopter emits shift to OIDC attestation eliminating the rotation cliff for that path. DECISIONS.md header reservation note (lines 12–21) precedes the decision table and correctly binds Codex executors. However fix-round-1 introduces one new MAJ bypass surface: the OIDC attestation architectural commitment specifies 'verifies against GitHub's OIDC JWKS' — JWKS verification is signature-only and proves only that GitHub issued the JWT. It does not constrain which workflow produced the attested artifact. Without an explicit requirement that the aggregator also verify the job_workflow_ref OIDC claim against the expected SCP reusable workflow path and SHA pin, a malicious opted-in adopter can use any workflow in their repo to generate a fabricated scorecard-emit.json with verdict:allow, attest it via gh attestation, and have the aggregator accept it — directly bypassing the only emit-integrity control introduced by fix-round-1. D-042's reservation block in §9 does not pre-constrain this verification requirement, leaving a Codex executor dispatched for 023C free to implement JWKS-signature-only verification. Two MIN findings and one nit also identified. NEVER recommend descoping.
